source: Adapted revision checklist based on VCAA's VCE Politics Study Design, Units 3 and 4 from 2025. Checklist numbers are internal tracker IDs. The course requires contemporary examples and case studies from within the last 10 years; older evidence should be used only to contextualise contemporary causes.
practiceNote: These practice questions and marking guides are original revision exercises, not VCAA examination questions. Adapt case-study answers to the global issue, humanitarian crisis, selected Indo-Pacific state and three Australian regional relationships taught by your school, using current evidence.
papers: Use the current VCAA Politics examination specifications, sample examination, past examinations and examination reports for official assessment resources.

points.area: Core concepts and contemporary politics
points.title: Global actors
points.detail: States, regional groupings, institutions of global governance and non-state actors, including the defining features and political roles of each category.

questions.q: Distinguish the four categories of global actor used in VCE Politics and give an example of each.
answer: States have territory, a permanent population and widely recognised sovereignty; Australia is one example.
Regional groupings are formal associations of states in a region, such as ASEAN or the Pacific Islands Forum.
Institutions of global governance have global scope and help states cooperate, enforce rules or resolve disputes; the United Nations is one example.
Non-state actors include transnational corporations, individuals, NGOs, terrorist groups and international criminal networks.

card.title: Global actors
back: States, regional groupings, institutions of global governance and non-state actors, including the defining features and political roles of each category.

points.area: Core concepts and contemporary politics
points.title: Interests and perspectives
points.detail: Interests as the outcomes actors seek and perspectives as the ways actors understand an issue, shaped by values, experience, identity and political circumstances.

questions.q: Explain the difference between an actor’s interests and perspectives and why the distinction matters.
answer: An interest is an outcome or advantage an actor seeks, such as security, prosperity or influence.
A perspective is the actor’s interpretation of an issue, shaped by values, identity, evidence and experience.
Actors can share an interest while holding different perspectives on how it should be achieved.
Distinguishing them helps explain why actors cooperate in some areas but conflict over methods or priorities.

card.title: Interests and perspectives
back: Interests as the outcomes actors seek and perspectives as the ways actors understand an issue, shaped by values, experience, identity and political circumstances.

points.area: Core concepts and contemporary politics
points.title: Sovereignty and the state
points.detail: Sovereignty as a state’s authority over its territory and population, and the ways global issues, laws, institutions and other actors can constrain state action.

questions.q: Define sovereignty and explain two ways it can be constrained in contemporary politics.
answer: Sovereignty is a state’s supreme authority over its territory and population and its recognised independence from other states.
International agreements constrain action when a state accepts common rules or dispute procedures.
Transnational problems such as climate change, financial instability and mass displacement cross borders and cannot be controlled by one state alone.
Powerful states, corporations or armed groups may also limit a government’s practical capacity to exercise authority.

card.title: Sovereignty and the state
back: Sovereignty as a state’s authority over its territory and population, and the ways global issues, laws, institutions and other actors can constrain state action.

points.area: Core concepts and contemporary politics
points.title: Political stability and change
points.detail: Political stability as the maintenance of institutions, relationships and order, and political change as significant alteration to authority, policy, relationships or institutions.

questions.q: Distinguish political stability from political change and explain why the same response may produce both.
answer: Political stability is the maintenance of political order, functioning institutions and predictable relationships.
Political change is a significant alteration to policies, institutions, power relationships or patterns of cooperation and conflict.
A response can stabilise one actor or region while changing another relationship or institution.
A strong answer identifies who experiences stability or change, the mechanism and the supporting evidence.

card.title: Political stability and change
back: Political stability as the maintenance of institutions, relationships and order, and political change as significant alteration to authority, policy, relationships or institutions.

points.area: Core concepts and contemporary politics
points.title: Cooperation, conflict and disengagement
points.detail: Cooperation as coordinated action, conflict as incompatible interests or actions, and disengagement as withdrawal or refusal to participate.

questions.q: Explain cooperation, conflict and disengagement as possible responses by global actors.
answer: Cooperation occurs when actors coordinate policies, resources or institutions to pursue a shared outcome.
Conflict occurs when actors’ interests, perspectives or actions are incompatible and produce political contest or confrontation.
Disengagement occurs when an actor withdraws, refuses to participate or limits involvement.
An actor may combine all three responses across different parts or stages of the same issue.

card.title: Cooperation, conflict and disengagement
back: Cooperation as coordinated action, conflict as incompatible interests or actions, and disengagement as withdrawal or refusal to participate.

points.area: Core concepts and contemporary politics
points.title: Global interconnectedness
points.detail: The political consequences of flows of trade, finance, information, people, technology and environmental effects across borders.

questions.q: Explain how global interconnectedness can both assist and obstruct the resolution of a political issue.
answer: Interconnectedness spreads information, expertise, finance and coordinated pressure, making joint responses possible.
It also transmits economic, security and environmental consequences rapidly between actors.
Actors become mutually dependent, so unilateral action may be ineffective or costly.
Different exposure to costs and benefits creates competing interests that can obstruct agreement.

card.title: Global interconnectedness
back: The political consequences of flows of trade, finance, information, people, technology and environmental effects across borders.

points.area: Core concepts and contemporary politics
points.title: Contemporary evidence and the 10-year rule
points.detail: The requirement that the central examples and case studies come from the last 10 years, with older events used only to contextualise contemporary causes and actions.

questions.q: How should evidence older than 10 years be used in VCE Politics?
answer: Use older evidence briefly to establish historical background or long-term causes.
Keep the analytical focus on short-term causes, responses and consequences from within the last 10 years.
Current examples should carry the argument because Politics is assessed as a contemporary study.

card.title: Contemporary evidence and the 10-year rule
back: The requirement that the central examples and case studies come from the last 10 years, with older events used only to contextualise contemporary causes and actions.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 1: Global issues, global responses
points.title: Selecting a global issue
points.detail: One issue must be studied in depth: climate change, global economic instability, development or weapons of mass destruction.

questions.q: What makes an issue suitable for Unit 3 Area of Study 1, and which four issues may be selected?
answer: The issue must be global in scale, transcend national and regional boundaries and be significant to multiple global actors.
The four prescribed options are climate change, global economic instability, development and weapons of mass destruction.
The course studies one option in depth rather than surveying all four.
Evidence must focus on contemporary causes, actor responses, challenges and consequences.

card.title: Selecting a global issue
back: One issue must be studied in depth: climate change, global economic instability, development or weapons of mass destruction.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 1: Global issues, global responses
points.title: Short-term causes of a global issue
points.detail: Political, economic, social, environmental, ideological, cultural and technological causes operating within the last 10 years.

questions.q: Analyse two short-term causes of your selected global issue.
answer: Identify two distinct causes from within the last 10 years and support each with specific evidence.
Explain the mechanism by which each cause intensified, spread or obstructed resolution of the issue.
Link the causes where appropriate rather than treating them as isolated facts.
Separate contemporary causes from older background conditions.

card.title: Short-term causes of a global issue
card.front: Short-term causes of a global issue
back: Political, economic, social, environmental, ideological, cultural and technological causes operating within the last 10 years.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 1: Global issues, global responses
points.title: Interconnectedness and the selected issue
points.detail: How cross-border flows and dependencies shape the causes, consequences and possible resolution of the chosen global issue.

questions.q: Assess the impact of global interconnectedness on your selected issue.
answer: Identify a specific cross-border connection, such as trade, finance, technology, migration or environmental effects.
Explain how it changes the scale, speed or distribution of the issue’s consequences.
Explain whether it improves cooperation or creates further competing interests.
Reach a judgement about its overall political impact using contemporary evidence.

card.title: Interconnectedness and the selected issue
back: How cross-border flows and dependencies shape the causes, consequences and possible resolution of the chosen global issue.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 1: Global issues, global responses
points.title: Global actor responses to an issue
points.detail: Responses by states, at least one institution of global governance and at least one non-state actor, including cooperation, conflict and disengagement.

questions.q: Compare the responses of a state, an institution of global governance and a non-state actor to your selected issue.
answer: For each actor, identify a specific policy, action or decision and the interest it was intended to advance.
Explain whether the response involved cooperation, conflict or disengagement.
Compare the actors’ authority, resources and ability to influence other actors.
Use evidence to judge which response contributed most effectively to addressing the issue.

card.title: Global actor responses to an issue
card.front: Global actor responses to an issue
back: Responses by states, at least one institution of global governance and at least one non-state actor, including cooperation, conflict and disengagement.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 1: Global issues, global responses
points.title: International law and global issues
points.detail: Treaties, declarations, agreements and decisions that establish expectations or obligations, and the extent to which actors comply with and enforce them.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of international law in addressing your selected global issue.
answer: Identify the relevant law, treaty, declaration, agreement or binding decision and what it requires.
Use evidence of compliance or changed behaviour to show effectiveness.
Use evidence of non-compliance, weak enforcement or limited participation to show constraints.
Judge effectiveness against the law’s objectives rather than merely stating that it exists.

card.title: International law and global issues
back: Treaties, declarations, agreements and decisions that establish expectations or obligations, and the extent to which actors comply with and enforce them.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 1: Global issues, global responses
points.title: Challenges to resolving a global issue
points.detail: Competing actor interests and perspectives, limits of law and institutions, sovereignty, unequal capabilities and the effects of interconnectedness.

questions.q: Discuss the major challenges to resolving your selected global issue.
answer: Explain at least two distinct challenges and support each with contemporary evidence.
Link each challenge to the interests, perspectives or capabilities of particular actors.
Show how the challenge obstructs cooperation, implementation or enforcement.
Weigh the challenges and identify which most seriously limits resolution.

card.title: Challenges to resolving a global issue
card.front: Challenges to resolving a global issue
back: Competing actor interests and perspectives, limits of law and institutions, sovereignty, unequal capabilities and the effects of interconnectedness.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 1: Global issues, global responses
points.title: Significance, effectiveness and political consequences
points.detail: Evaluation of the issue’s political significance, actors’ ability to respond and the resulting political stability and change.

questions.q: Evaluate the ability of global actors to respond effectively to your selected issue.
answer: Establish criteria for effectiveness, such as progress toward resolution, compliance, reach, durability and unintended consequences.
Compare the actions and capabilities of the required actor categories using specific evidence.
Explain how the responses produced political stability and/or change for identified actors.
Reach a qualified overall judgement that recognises both achievement and limitation.

card.title: Significance, effectiveness and political consequences
back: Evaluation of the issue’s political significance, actors’ ability to respond and the resulting political stability and change.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 2: Contemporary crises: conflict, stability and change
points.title: Selecting a contemporary humanitarian crisis
points.detail: One significant crisis must be studied from human rights, armed conflict or the mass movement of people, affecting large numbers and concerning multiple states.

questions.q: What makes a crisis suitable for Unit 3 Area of Study 2?
answer: It must fall within human rights, armed conflict or the mass movement of people.
It must be significant in scale, affect large numbers of people and concern several states.
Although it may originate within one state, its consequences must extend beyond that state.
The main causes, responses and evidence must be contemporary and generally within the last 10 years.

card.title: Selecting a contemporary humanitarian crisis
back: One significant crisis must be studied from human rights, armed conflict or the mass movement of people, affecting large numbers and concerning multiple states.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 2: Contemporary crises: conflict, stability and change
points.title: Short-term causes of a contemporary crisis
points.detail: Immediate and interacting causes within the last 10 years, including discrimination, sovereignty disputes, resource conflict, poverty, climate pressures and armed violence.

questions.q: Analyse two short-term causes of your selected humanitarian crisis.
answer: Identify two specific causes operating within the last 10 years.
Explain how each cause contributed to the outbreak, escalation or spread of the crisis.
Show how actor interests or perspectives shaped at least one cause.
Use older events only where necessary to clarify the contemporary context.

card.title: Short-term causes of a contemporary crisis
card.front: Short-term causes of a contemporary crisis
back: Immediate and interacting causes within the last 10 years, including discrimination, sovereignty disputes, resource conflict, poverty, climate pressures and armed violence.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 2: Contemporary crises: conflict, stability and change
points.title: Actors’ perspectives and interests in a crisis
points.detail: How different understandings, priorities and desired outcomes shape the course of a crisis and actors’ willingness to cooperate.

questions.q: Compare the perspectives and interests of two global actors involved in your selected crisis.
answer: State each actor’s perspective and the evidence or values shaping it.
Identify the security, political, economic or humanitarian interest each actor pursues.
Explain how the difference affects the actor’s actions or response.
Conclude whether the competing positions primarily drive conflict or still permit cooperation.

card.title: Actors’ perspectives and interests in a crisis
card.front: Actors’ perspectives and interests in a crisis
back: How different understandings, priorities and desired outcomes shape the course of a crisis and actors’ willingness to cooperate.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 2: Contemporary crises: conflict, stability and change
points.title: Responses by global and regional actors
points.detail: Responses by states, an institution of global governance and/or regional grouping, and a non-state actor.

questions.q: Analyse the responses of three different actor types to your selected crisis.
answer: Use a state, an institution of global governance or regional grouping, and a non-state actor.
Identify the concrete response taken by each and the interest or objective behind it.
Explain the political mechanism through which each response was intended to affect the crisis.
Compare their reach, authority, resources and observable outcomes.

card.title: Responses by global and regional actors
card.front: Responses by global and regional actors
back: Responses by states, an institution of global governance and/or regional grouping, and a non-state actor.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 2: Contemporary crises: conflict, stability and change
points.title: Diplomacy and international law
points.detail: Negotiation, mediation, agreements, legal obligations, courts, investigations and other processes used to manage or resolve a crisis.

questions.q: Evaluate the contribution of diplomacy and international law to addressing your selected crisis.
answer: Identify a specific diplomatic process and a relevant international legal rule or institution.
Explain what each process achieved, using evidence rather than intention alone.
Analyse constraints such as lack of consent, enforcement, trust or agreement among powerful actors.
Judge whether they reduced harm, changed behaviour or advanced a durable resolution.

card.title: Diplomacy and international law
back: Negotiation, mediation, agreements, legal obligations, courts, investigations and other processes used to manage or resolve a crisis.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 2: Contemporary crises: conflict, stability and change
points.title: Challenges to crisis resolution
points.detail: Competing interests, sovereignty, limited enforcement, resource constraints, disagreement over facts or responsibility and the continuation of violence.

questions.q: Discuss the challenges that prevent effective resolution of your selected crisis.
answer: Explain at least two challenges and identify the actors connected to each.
Show how each challenge limits cooperation, access, enforcement or implementation.
Support the analysis with recent and specific evidence from the selected crisis.
Weigh which challenge has had the greatest effect on prospects for resolution.

card.title: Challenges to crisis resolution
back: Competing interests, sovereignty, limited enforcement, resource constraints, disagreement over facts or responsibility and the continuation of violence.

points.area: Unit 3: Global cooperation and conflict — AoS 2: Contemporary crises: conflict, stability and change
points.title: Crisis consequences, significance and change
points.detail: The human and political consequences of the crisis and the extent to which actor responses produce political stability or change.

questions.q: Evaluate the political significance of your selected crisis and the effectiveness of responses to it.
answer: Explain consequences for affected populations, states, regional relationships and relevant institutions.
Assess responses against clear criteria such as protection, access, de-escalation, accountability and durability.
Identify evidence of both political stability and political change caused by the crisis or responses.
Reach a supported judgement about significance and effectiveness rather than listing events.

card.title: Crisis consequences, significance and change
back: The human and political consequences of the crisis and the extent to which actor responses produce political stability or change.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 1: Power and the national interest
points.title: The Indo-Pacific and the selected state
points.detail: The prescribed regional definition and the in-depth study of China, Japan, India, Indonesia or the United States.

questions.q: Define the Indo-Pacific for VCE Politics and name the five states available for in-depth study.
answer: The Indo-Pacific extends from the eastern Indian Ocean to the Pacific Ocean, connected through Southeast Asia.
It includes India, North Asia, Southeast Asia, Pacific states, Australia and the United States.
The selected state must be China, Japan, India, Indonesia or the United States.
One state is studied in depth through its power, interests, actions, challenges and regional consequences.

card.title: The Indo-Pacific and the selected state
card.front: The Indo-Pacific and the selected state
back: The prescribed regional definition and the in-depth study of China, Japan, India, Indonesia or the United States.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 1: Power and the national interest
points.title: Sources and forms of state power
points.detail: Political, economic, military, diplomatic and cultural power, including the distinction between the resources a state possesses and how it uses them.

questions.q: Analyse three forms of power used by your selected Indo-Pacific state.
answer: Identify three of political, economic, military, diplomatic and cultural power with specific evidence.
Explain the source of each capability, such as institutions, markets, armed forces, relationships or cultural reach.
Analyse how the state converts the capability into influence over another actor.
Do not assume a large capability is effective without showing an outcome.

card.title: Sources and forms of state power
card.front: Sources and forms of state power
back: Political, economic, military, diplomatic and cultural power, including the distinction between the resources a state possesses and how it uses them.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 1: Power and the national interest
points.title: Four national interests
points.detail: Security, economic prosperity, regional relationships and regional standing as multifaceted and changeable guides to state policy.

questions.q: Explain the four national interests examined for the selected Indo-Pacific state.
answer: Security concerns protection of the state, population, sovereignty and strategic environment.
Economic prosperity concerns trade, investment, resources, growth and material wellbeing.
Regional relationships concern maintaining useful and stable connections with other regional actors.
Regional standing concerns status, reputation and influence in shaping the regional order.

card.title: Four national interests
back: Security, economic prosperity, regional relationships and regional standing as multifaceted and changeable guides to state policy.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 1: Power and the national interest
points.title: Foreign policy instruments
points.detail: Diplomacy, trade and foreign aid as required instruments, used alongside wider applications of political, economic, military, diplomatic and cultural power.

questions.q: Compare diplomacy, trade and foreign aid as instruments used by your selected state.
answer: Diplomacy uses negotiation, representation and agreements to communicate and coordinate policy.
Trade uses market access, agreements, restrictions or economic dependence to create benefit or leverage.
Foreign aid transfers resources or expertise and can support development, relationships and influence.
Compare how the state used each instrument and the national interest it was intended to advance.

card.title: Foreign policy instruments
back: Diplomacy, trade and foreign aid as required instruments, used alongside wider applications of political, economic, military, diplomatic and cultural power.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 1: Power and the national interest
points.title: Effectiveness in achieving national interests
points.detail: The degree to which actions deliver stated outcomes, considering resistance, trade-offs, duration and unintended consequences.

questions.q: Evaluate how effectively your selected state has achieved one national interest.
answer: Define the national interest and identify the outcomes the state sought.
Use at least two actions or instruments and evidence of their results.
Consider resistance, costs, trade-offs and unintended consequences as limits on effectiveness.
Reach a qualified judgement based on the extent and durability of achievement.

card.title: Effectiveness in achieving national interests
back: The degree to which actions deliver stated outcomes, considering resistance, trade-offs, duration and unintended consequences.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 1: Power and the national interest
points.title: Challenges to the selected state
points.detail: Domestic and regional constraints that inhibit the pursuit of national interests, including competing actors, limited resources, geography and conflicting priorities.

questions.q: Analyse two challenges faced by your selected state in pursuing its national interests.
answer: Identify each challenge precisely and support it with contemporary evidence.
Explain the mechanism by which it limits a policy, instrument or desired outcome.
Connect the challenge to a particular national interest rather than discussing it generally.
Compare the seriousness of the challenges or explain how they interact.

card.title: Challenges to the selected state
back: Domestic and regional constraints that inhibit the pursuit of national interests, including competing actors, limited resources, geography and conflicting priorities.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 1: Power and the national interest
points.title: Consequences for other regional actors
points.detail: Intended and unintended effects of at least two national interests on other states, institutions, groupings or non-state actors.

questions.q: Analyse the consequences of two of your selected state’s national interests for other regional actors.
answer: Use two distinct national interests and identify the regional actors affected by each.
Explain the causal link between the state’s action and each consequence.
Consider positive and negative, intended and unintended consequences where supported.
Show how those consequences affect cooperation, conflict, stability or change.

card.title: Consequences for other regional actors
back: Intended and unintended effects of at least two national interests on other states, institutions, groupings or non-state actors.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 1: Power and the national interest
points.title: Regional stability, change and political significance
points.detail: The extent to which the selected state’s actions and national-interest outcomes shape the regional distribution of influence, relationships and political order.

questions.q: Evaluate the political significance of your selected state’s pursuit of its national interests.
answer: Explain how its actions affect regional influence, relationships, institutions or strategic behaviour.
Use evidence of both stability and change, identifying the actors affected.
Evaluate effectiveness as well as consequences; a significant action is not necessarily a successful one.
Reach an overall judgement about the state’s importance to the contemporary Indo-Pacific.

card.title: Regional stability, change and political significance
card.front: Regional stability, change and political significance
back: The extent to which the selected state’s actions and national-interest outcomes shape the regional distribution of influence, relationships and political order.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 2: Australia in the Indo-Pacific
points.title: Australia’s national interests
points.detail: Security, economic prosperity, regional relationships and regional standing as drivers of Australian policy in the Indo-Pacific.

questions.q: Explain Australia’s four national interests in the Indo-Pacific.
answer: Security includes territorial protection, a favourable strategic environment and resilience against regional threats.
Economic prosperity includes trade, investment, stable markets and secure supply chains.
Regional relationships involve trusted and productive ties with neighbouring states and groupings.
Regional standing concerns Australia’s reputation, legitimacy and influence in regional decisions.

card.title: Australia’s national interests
back: Security, economic prosperity, regional relationships and regional standing as drivers of Australian policy in the Indo-Pacific.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 2: Australia in the Indo-Pacific
points.title: Internal and external perspectives on Australia
points.detail: Different views within Australia and among regional actors about Australia’s interests, identity, alliances, priorities and conduct.

questions.q: Compare one internal and one external perspective on an Australian national interest.
answer: Identify who holds each perspective and the values, interests or experience shaping it.
Explain how the internal perspective defines the Australian interest or preferred action.
Explain how the external actor interprets Australia’s objective or behaviour.
Analyse how the difference affects trust, cooperation or conflict.

card.title: Internal and external perspectives on Australia
card.front: Internal and external perspectives on Australia
back: Different views within Australia and among regional actors about Australia’s interests, identity, alliances, priorities and conduct.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 2: Australia in the Indo-Pacific
points.title: Australian forms of power
points.detail: Australia’s political, economic, military, diplomatic and cultural capabilities and how they are applied to influence regional actors.

questions.q: Analyse three forms of power Australia uses in the Indo-Pacific.
answer: Identify three forms of power and support each with a specific contemporary example.
Explain the capability or relationship that gives Australia that form of power.
Analyse how it is used to influence another actor or regional outcome.
Evaluate limits such as dependence, credibility, scale or competing regional powers.

card.title: Australian forms of power
back: Australia’s political, economic, military, diplomatic and cultural capabilities and how they are applied to influence regional actors.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 2: Australia in the Indo-Pacific
points.title: Australian foreign policy instruments
points.detail: Diplomacy, trade and foreign aid as required instruments for pursuing Australian interests and managing regional relationships.

questions.q: Compare Australia’s use of diplomacy, trade and foreign aid in the Indo-Pacific.
answer: Identify a specific contemporary use of each required instrument.
Connect each use to one or more Australian national interests.
Explain how each instrument encourages cooperation or creates leverage.
Compare their effectiveness and any costs or tensions they produce.

card.title: Australian foreign policy instruments
back: Diplomacy, trade and foreign aid as required instruments for pursuing Australian interests and managing regional relationships.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 2: Australia in the Indo-Pacific
points.title: The three-state case-study requirement
points.detail: Australia’s relationships with one Pacific Islands Forum member and two other Indo-Pacific states, studied through cooperation, challenges and policy consequences.

questions.q: What three state relationships must be studied for Australia in the Indo-Pacific?
answer: One selected state must be a member of the Pacific Islands Forum.
Two additional selected states must come from the wider Indo-Pacific region.
For all three, study cooperation, competing interests, perspectives and challenges in the bilateral relationship.
Use distinct and current evidence for each relationship rather than treating the region as a single actor.

card.title: The three-state case-study requirement
back: Australia’s relationships with one Pacific Islands Forum member and two other Indo-Pacific states, studied through cooperation, challenges and policy consequences.

points.area: Unit 4: Power in the Indo-Pacific — AoS 2: Australia in the Indo-Pacific
points.title: Challenges to Australia’s regional relationships
points.detail: Strategic competition, historical experience, climate priorities, economic dependence, human rights, sovereignty and different perceptions of Australia’s role.

questions.q: Analyse two challenges to Australia’s relationship with one selected regional state.
answer: Identify two specific challenges and the interests or perspectives underlying them.
Explain how each challenge affects policy coordination, trust or another form of cooperation.
Use evidence from both Australia and the selected state where possible.
Judge which challenge has had the greater effect on the relationship.

card.title: Challenges to Australia’s regional relationships
back: Strategic competition, historical experience, climate priorities, economic dependence, human rights, sovereignty and different perceptions of Australia’s role.

Explain how the selected regional state perceived or experienced that response.
Use evidence to assess whether it increased cooperation, conflict or both.

card.front: Responses to a regional issue or crisis

answer: Compare evidence from the three selected state relationships rather than relying on a single case.
Assess Australia’s use of power and instruments against clear national-interest outcomes.
Explain contributions to both political stability and political change in identified relationships or institutions.
Reach a qualified judgement that accounts for regional perspectives and unintended consequences.

card.title: Australia’s contribution to stability and change
card.front: Australia’s contribution to stability and change

points.area: Evidence and exam technique
points.title: Building a contemporary evidence bank
points.detail: Organising dated actions, actors, interests, perspectives, outcomes and evaluative significance for every selected issue, crisis and state relationship.

questions.q: What should a useful Politics evidence bank record for each example?
answer: Record the date, actor and concrete action or decision.
Identify the actor’s interest and perspective, supported by a reliable source.
Record the observable outcome and any competing interpretation of its significance.
Link the evidence to a specific key-knowledge point and update it as events change.

card.title: Building a contemporary evidence bank
back: Organising dated actions, actors, interests, perspectives, outcomes and evaluative significance for every selected issue, crisis and state relationship.

points.area: Evidence and exam technique
points.title: Analysing sources and perspectives
points.detail: Testing a source’s origin, purpose, evidence and perspective, then corroborating claims rather than accepting political language at face value.

questions.q: Explain how to analyse a political source rather than merely quote it.
answer: Identify the author, context, audience and purpose and how these shape the source’s perspective.
Extract the political claim and the evidence offered for it.
Compare it with another reliable source or actor perspective to test accuracy and significance.
Use the source as evidence within your own analysis instead of substituting quotation for explanation.

back: Testing a source’s origin, purpose, evidence and perspective, then corroborating claims rather than accepting political language at face value.

questions.q: Distinguish analyse, discuss and evaluate in a VCE Politics response.
answer: Analyse requires breaking an issue into parts and explaining relationships, causes and consequences.
Discuss requires a balanced examination of relevant arguments, evidence or perspectives.
Evaluate requires criteria, evidence on strengths and limits, and a supported judgement.
In every case, follow the exact object of the command and use the mark allocation to judge required depth.

questions.q: Outline a strong structure for an extended evaluative Politics response.
answer: State a contention that directly answers the question and establishes the basis for judgement.
Organise paragraphs around analytical claims, each supported by precise contemporary evidence.
Compare relevant actors, interests and perspectives and test evidence against explicit criteria.
Sustain evaluation throughout and finish with a qualified judgement about extent, significance or effectiveness.
